about: The integral theorems of vector analysis for TU Wien's Mathematik 3 for electrical engineering. Taschner's own text for that course, Anwendungsorientierte Mathematik, Band 3 (Hanser), was not available; the labs follow the free lecture notes of Fritzsche (2003), Mathematik 3 für Elektrotechnik und IT, Bergische Universität Wuppertal, chapter 9 § 2 and chapter 10 §§ 1, 3 and 4, by section and printed page, read from the page images on 2 Nov 2026. Fritzsche numbers no equations, so each is cited by its page. Practice answers are worked by hand or taken from Fritzsche's examples; tests/unit/labs-data.test.js recomputes each with the core. Maxwell's equations are in the Electrodynamics Lab.

labs.title: Line integrals and potentials
labs.idea: Walk through a field from p to q and add up F along the way. In a gradient field every path gives the same, f(q) − f(p), and a closed loop gives zero; in a swirling field the path matters.

equations.note: the line integral of F along the path α: what the lab adds up, step by step

equations.eq: F = ∇f  ⇔  ∫α F • dx path-independent  ⇔  ∮ F • dx = 0
equations.tex: \mathbf{F} = \nabla f \;\Leftrightarrow\; \int_\alpha \mathbf{F} \bullet d\mathbf{x} \text{ independent of the path} \;\Leftrightarrow\; \oint \mathbf{F} \bullet d\mathbf{x} = 0
equations.note: the main theorem on line integrals (Hauptsatz über Kurvenintegrale), on a domain G
a gradient field's integral is the difference of its potential f at the ends

equations.eq: F = (−y, x, 0)/(x² + y²): ∮ round the origin = 2π
equations.note: the vortex: curl-free, yet no gradient field on the plane without the origin

practice.question: The vortex F = (−y, x, 0)/(x² + y²) is integrated once round the unit circle, counter-clockwise. What is ∮ F • dx?
practice.solution: On α(t) = (cos t, sin t, 0), F(α(t)) • α'(t) = sin² t + cos² t = 1, so the integral is ∫₀^2π dt = 2π ≈ 6.283.

practice.question: In the gradient field F = ∇f with f = x² − y², what is ∫ F • dx from p = (−1.2, −0.6) to q = (1.2, 0.9), on any path?
practice.source: Worked by hand from the main theorem, Fritzsche (2003), p. 22

labs.title: Circulation and curl: Green and Stokes
labs.idea: Run round the edge of a surface and add up F along it: the circulation. Stokes' theorem says it equals the curl added up over the surface inside. In the plane this is Green's theorem.

equations.eq: ∮∂G F • dx = ∫G (g_x − f_y) dx dy,  F = (f, g)
equations.note: Green's theorem, for a Jordan domain G and F continuously differentiable round it; ∂G runs with G on its left
Stokes' theorem for a surface S in space with edge bS; for a flat S in the plane it is Green's theorem

equations.eq: w_F(x0, n) = lim ε→0 (1/A(S_ε)) ∫bS_ε F • dx = rot F • n
equations.note: the circulation of a small disc per area, the vortex density (Wirbeldichte), is the curl along its normal
Green's theorem gives the area of G from its edge alone: the rotation field (−y, x) has curl 2

practice.question: The rotation field F = (−y, x, 0) is integrated once round a circle of radius 1, counter-clockwise. What is ∮ F • dx?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Fritzsche (2003), p. 63, example 1: v₂ of the disc is πr²
practice.solution: By Green, ∮ F • dx = ∫ (g_x − f_y) dx dy = ∫ 2 dx dy = 2 · π · 1² = 2π ≈ 6.283. Fritzsche's p. 63 has ½ ∮ (x dy − y dx) = πr².

labs.title: Flux and divergence: Gauss
labs.idea: Add up how much of F flows out through a closed surface: the flux. Gauss's theorem says it equals the divergence, the sources, added up over the volume inside.

equations.note: Gauss's theorem, for a domain Ω with piecewise smooth boundary and F continuously differentiable round it

equations.tex: \mathbf{div}\,F = \frac{\partial F_1}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial F_2}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial F_3}{\partial z}
equations.note: the divergence of a field in space

equations.eq: δ_F(x0) = lim ε→0 (1/v₃(B_ε)) ∫∂B_ε F • dO = div F(x0)
equations.note: the flux out of a small ball per volume, the source density (Quelldichte), is the divergence

practice.question: The source field F = (x, y, 0) streams out of a sphere of radius 1 about the origin. What is the flux ∫ F • dO?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Gauss's theorem, Fritzsche (2003), p. 85
practice.solution: div F = 1 + 1 + 0 = 2 everywhere, so the flux is 2 times the volume of the ball: 2 · (4/3)π · 1³ = 8π/3 ≈ 8.378.
